https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-s-lake-vel.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IHL4 Lake Velence's water levels have dropped to a record low Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Advertisement A dead fish lies half-decayed on the shore. Its eyes have been picked out by the birds. Hungary's Lake Velence will likely experience a massive fish kill. That's because oxygen levels in the body of water are too low, according to environmental experts. This means more and more fish will suffocate. Hungary has seen temperatures soar to 40 degrees Celsius, with barely any rain. This heat is having a major impact on the country's third-largest natural lake. Its water has never been particularly deep, but the current situation is dire. Water levels have been recorded in Agard, on the southern shore, since 1933. It dropped to a historic low in September 2022, measuring just 53 centimeters. Yet as of today, August 4, the water level has dropped to a mere 29 centimeters (11 inches). As long as it doesn't rain and temperatures remain hot, the water level will continue to drop every day, by half a centimeter per day on average. The water is currently evaporating at such a fast pace that there may soon be no continuous body of water left, only isolated pools. This could mark a critical tipping point for the lake. The impact of Hungary's ongoing drought is already clearly visible. The lake has receded by dozens of meters. Ground once covered in water is now so dry that the soil is cracking. The reed belt surrounding the lake, which serves as a habitat for numerous bird species, is now largely rooted in dry soil. But not all living creatures are suffering under the current conditions: that's evident from a constant hum in the air near the water's edge. As fish and aquatic plants find their habitats shrinking, flies, bacteria, and other decomposers take over, breaking down what the drought leaves behind. No swimming The water shortage isn't just changing the lake — it's changing the entire region. Lake Velence is a popular tourist destination, located just 50 kilometers from Hungary's capital, Budapest. It is considered less crowded than nearby Lake Balaton. Swimming is not an option this summer at Lake Velence Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW But these days, there are barely any visitors. The remaining water has turned a brownish-green and taken on a slightly musty odor. A "No Swimming" sign has been put up, with yellow tape blocking access to the water. Five swimming spots have been closed to the public since July 23. The Velence municipal government says the beach will only reopen once the lake's water quality improves, though it is unclear when that might happen. The persistent heat and low water levels mean the lake's water is getting warmer and warmer, leading to a growth in bacteria and blue-green algae. Tourist industry under pressure The people living around the lake, who make their living in the region's tourist sector, are hard hit by the lake's falling water levels. Today, only one family is visiting the northern beach — not for swimming but sunbathing. There is a water slide, slowly rusting away, with the end of the chute not even reaching the water anymore. Only one kiosk is open today. A woman is selling langos, Hungary's well-known fried bread, as well as ice cream and lemonade. "The slide hasn't been used for years," the saleswoman tells DW. "It really needs fixing, but who will pay for it when fewer and fewer tourists come here?" Campsites and holiday homes around the lake seem deserted, with many stores closed. Peggy Barath works in an ice cream shop on Velence Promenade, telling DW, "We've always had a lot of tourists here." She says many visitors were from East Germany , the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. But in recent years, their numbers have been dwindling "because of the lake's low water levels." Peggy Barath hopes the situation will improve and tourists will return Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Peggy says that the ice cream shop now focuses on cyclists rather than tourists looking to swim, as cyclists are undeterred by low water levels. No long-term solution in sight Major interventions in the region's water cycle have made the lake more vulnerable to droughts over the years. "The lakeshore has been subject to significant construction activity over the past 15 years," Zoltan Kun, president of the Hungarian Great Lakes and Wetlands Association, tells DW. "The water management authority has focused on quickly draining excess water from the region rather than storing it using nature-based solutions. And the agricultural industry destroyed our soils, which means they are less able to absorb water." This isn't the first time Lake Velence has dried up. When this happened in the early 1990s, the lake was replenished with water from various other sources, a solution that proved effective but also expensive and time-consuming. That's why experts are calling for a more sustainable solution today, especially since climate change means more drought periods are expected. The Zamolyi and Patkai reservoirs could, for instance, be renovated so that water could be stored there during periods of heavy rainfall. During dry spells, this water could then be diverted into Lake Valance. The dry, cracked bed of Hungary's third-largest lake Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Yet little has happened so far. In 2021, the government at the time, led by Prime Minister Viktor Orban , rejected a broad investment program for the lake on the grounds that it was too costly. Other projects, however, went ahead. A new canoe center Although it has long been clear that water levels drop to a critical level in summer and fall, authorities built a brand-new canoeing center on the north shore between 2021 and 2024, suitable for international competitions. The project cost about 140 million euros in government funds. Lanes are marked off in the lake with buoys in front of the newly built spectator tower. It's very quiet, like elsewhere along the body of water. Floating docks sit low in the greenish-brown water. The World University Canoe Championships were supposed to be held here in August, the first major event to be staged at the newly built center. Yet due to persistently low water levels, the event was moved to Szeged, southern Hungary, instead. This means that for the time being, the Lake Velence facility remains nothing more than an expensive training center. A sandbank has formed in front of Budapest's Margaret Island Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Nuclear power plant on brink of shutdown Hungary's ongoing heat wave is being felt all over the country. Water levels of the Danube River have dropped significantly, exposing stretches of dry riverbed around Budapest's Margaret Island. Tourists and locals alike are taking in the unusual sight, snapping photos on a sandbar that has emerged off the island. The low water level has also attracted scrap-metal collectors, who use magnets to pull rusty metal objects from parts of the river that are normally submerged. The low water level has dramatic consequences. With the exception of a few sightseeing steamboats, boat traffic has almost ceased on the Danube River. Not only that. Paks nuclear power plant, located about 100 kilometers downstream from Budapest, can no longer be cooled with Danube water. The site's electricity output, which covers about half of Hungary's power consumption, has been gradually reduced over the past few days, and it is set to be shut down later this week for the first time ever. Hungary's power options after drought shuts nuclear plant To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "We are facing a crisis that is beyond our control and putting us to the test," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said at a joint press conference with Interim President Agnes Forsthoffer on Monday. He added that the next five days would be the most critical of the summer of 2026. Magyar has asked the Hungarian public to conserve electricity. Many companies have agreed to voluntarily reduce their power consumption. Some public buildings and bridges are no longer illuminated at night, and rail freight traffic is suspended between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. Hungary faces a very challenging time, with temperatures over 40 degrees Celsius expected over the next days. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/23/tigr.text: Tigrayan rebels in northern Ethiopia seized control of a key airport and clashed with federal troops in the neighbouring region of Afar on Wednesday, as long-standing tensions spilt into open battle.Fighting escalated "since last night in Abala and Erebti (in Afar) between TPLF and federal forces," an NGO source in the region said, requesting anonymity."We are expecting it to expand. We just sent a truck with food to help the people displaced," they added.Abala lies in the mountain ranges that mark the border with Tigray. Erebti lies around 100 kilometres further into Afar.Another humanitarian source confirmed clashes in the two locations, as did a foreign security source in Ethiopia.A former TPLF senior official said the rebels were in control of Berhale, Erebti, Abala, Megale, Dalul and Konoba in Afar.The federal forces are "fast-retreating", he added.Meanwhile, local and security sources said Tigrayan forces were in control of the airport in the regional capital Mekelle.Ethiopian Airlines said it had suspended flights to three airports in Tigray — Mekelle, Axum and Shire — "due to the current situation"."While we were on our way to the airport for work, our supervisor called the driver and told him that the airport had been taken over by Tigray forces. Since there were no flights, he told us to return home," an employee at Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle said.A foreign security source based in Ethiopia confirmed the information.A small number of federal police guard the airport and their situation was unknown.Between 2020 and 2022, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fought a devastating war with the federal government that resulted in the deaths of some 600,000 people, according to African Union estimates.Sporadic clashes in recent months have raised fears of a return to war.Abiy under fireEthiopia faces multiple insurgencies, including in its most populous regions, Oromia and Amhara.On Sunday, the TPLF announced it had joined a seven-group military alliance dubbed Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival aiming to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and install a transitional administration.The alliance also includes Amhara nationalist Fano militias — who fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF during the last war — and the Oromo Liberation Army, an active insurgency in Ethiopia's most populous region, along with four groups from three other regions, making up half of the country's 12 regional states.The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, which eventually triggered the war in 2020.The Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the war and maintained an uneasy calm until late 2025, when clashes resumed.The federal government has since launched drone strikes in Tigray and massed troops at the regional border.Rights groups have accused the TPLF of a campaign of forced recruitment this year as it prepares for renewed fighting.The region has not recovered from the last war, with around 1 million people still displaced and many parts of the peace deal unfulfilled.Abiy won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 partly for brokering a peace agreement with neighbouring Eritrea.Good friends and neighboursThe federal government has a significant military advantage, having ramped up production of military drones since the last war.Yet the TPLF's Tigray Defence Forces retain a significant inherited arsenal from their years at the helm of Ethiopia's military before 2018, including tanks, artillery, long-range guided rockets and ballistic missiles documented by open-source military analysts during the 2020-2022 war.Ethiopia's Foreign Minister Gedion Timotheos said in June that TPLF hardliners had been "actively accumulating and acquiring new arms" in violation of the Pretoria Agreement.Neighbouring countries have also been implicated in backing the rebels.ACLED conflict monitoring group assessed earlier this year that Eritrean forces had moved troops toward western Tigray in coordination with the TDF and that Eritrea was providing weapons and hosting Tigrayan fighters.Ethiopia's government formally accused Sudan's armed forces in May of providing "arms and financial support" to TPLF-linked forces and described Sudan as "a hub of anti-Ethiopian forces". Sudan denied the allegation.Locked in a long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, Egypt is assessed by analysts at the Soufan Center as providing diplomatic cover and logistical support to Ethiopian opposition factions, although no direct weapons transfers to the TPLF have been documented.

https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/09/12/explo.text: An explosion caused a fire at a weapons storage site in central Bulgaria overnight, local media and officials said on Saturday, the second blaze at a munitions facility in the past few weeks. No one was reported injured in the blaze, which broke out near the village of Tsareva Livada and could be seen lighting up the night sky in videos broadcast locally. “At the moment, the fire is on the territory of the storage base of the factory. It is moving from warehouse to warehouse,” Gabrovo regional governor Kristina Sidorova told journalists in the early hours of Saturday. Local media reported that the fire was at a site run by EMCO, which experienced an explosion at another facility last month, citing an EMCO company official. Reuters was not immediately able to reach EMCO for comment. EMCO is run by Bulgarian arms trader Emilian Gebrev, who Bulgarian prosecutors allege was the target of past attacks on his facilities by Russian operatives. In 2024, Bulgaria issued an arrest warrant for six Russian citizens accused of involvement in the destruction of EMCO arms depots that were storing munitions for export to Ukraine and Georgia between 2011 and 2020. Prosecutors at the time said that they could reasonably assume links between the blasts in Bulgaria, an attempted poisoning of Gebrev in 2015, and munitions depot explosions in the Czech Republic in 2014. Moscow has dismissed the allegations.

https://www.chroniclelive.co.uk/whats-on.text: Dumplings, sausage and 'farmer's cheese' are probably going to appeal to most of us, particularly when cold weather has us yearning for comfort food. And the new Restaurant Biedronka, opening in County Durham this Thursday, currently has those - and a whole lot more - on a tasting menu which sees owner-chef Marek Dziedzic out to introduce local diners to the kind of food he enjoyed while growing up in his native Poland. Biedronka, which means 'ladybird' in Polish, is Marek's first restaurant and it takes over The Farmhouse, a standalone old stone property in the grounds of South Causey Inn which boasts open views of the beautiful Beamish Valley countryside surrounding it. It was vacated in the summer by Hjem, where Marek worked before that restaurant's residency came to a close, and now he has an opportunity to showcase his culinary talents to the full - along with the flavours of the Polish countryside he left several years ago. It's an exciting time and he's full of enthusiasm about sharing new tastes and ingredients in his inspired take on traditional dishes which also make the most of seasonal British produce. A tasting menu allows him to do just that and diners can pick from between four and seven courses. There are four sections: snacks; starters and dumplings; seafood and meat, and desserts. On a visit ahead of opening day, sitting in the candle-lit dining room at a window where we could enjoy the last of the scenic view before a dark evening cut in, we started with bread and smalec. There are some dishes on the menu which may not initially appeal and smalec - pork fat - is one of them. Lard was common to us years ago but now hardly dares raise its head. This is pork fat seasoned with onions, garlic and apples and is to be spread on the bread after it has been butter, we're told, and then topped with slices of the restaurant's home-made pickles to cut through the fatty taste. And this turned out to be a taste sensation, even one of our favourite parts of the meal. It's not the sort of thing my dining companion would ever have chosen but, while not liking the sound of it, she wanted to give everything a go and she thought it was delicious. And so the rest of courses turned out. Those dumplings and sausages are different to what we're used to and the latter - a slice each of four dried Polish sausages, accompanied by cornichons and silverskin onions, had so much flavour and texture. A pastrami dish was another new-try for my guest and another surprise hit, with cavalo nero, anchovy and Parmesan adding to a myriad of flavours - not one of them overpowering. Another favourite of mine was Pierogi Ruskie - one of a wide variety of dumplings, including a dessert version, which will be on the menu - and this really was comfort food. It's where the farmer's cheese comes in and this is combined with potato to fill the dumplings whose dressing of brown butter, herbs and breadcrumbs added saltiness and extra depth. Marek, whose brother - over from Poland - was there to help out the kitchen team ahead of Thursday's launch, talks with real passion about his grandmother's version of Pierogi Ruskie which is a Poland staple, served regularly and often in even bigger portions he says. Then came a beautifully-colourful fish dish: brill with Shetland mussels and in its sauce, along with cider and pops of orange roe and green oil, there were haricot beans, lettuce - grilled apparently - and all sorts of tastes. The multi-course menu, which the restaurant says will change to reflect seasons, availablity and inspiration, is a real treat and full of surprise flavours - pickles more sweet than sharp, for instance. Even mushrooms had a unique flavour. Other dishes - which are all served on different, country-style-pattern crockery - included Lindisfarne oyster, topped with a cucumber and sorrel jelly, which is the only course my guest didn't manage, and roasted duck breast with red cabbage and beetroot - rich colours to match the taste - which came accompanied by a separate plate containing a duck leg-filled dumpling. It was quite some feast and along with it we had a lovely sparkling wine then I tried a glass of orange wine - from a wide drinks menu - which was recommended to go with the food by the serving staff who added hugely to the evening by describing each dish in detail as it was served. We were served a sorbet and really had no room for a dessert - I don't usually go for them - but who could resist a warm baked chocolate soufflé? I am in awe of anyone who can bake a soufflé and I spotted perfect creations being served simultaneously to tables across the room. The individual portions were far too big really but they were chocolatety perfection so I ate nearly all of mine and this time the surprise was the sour cream ice cream served on top. Yes, sour. It was certainly another taste combination we had never tried so, did it work? Of course it did. Restaurant Biedronka is an exciting new addition and diners are in for a journey of discovery. From this October 1, it will be offering two dinner servings, starting at £65 for four courses, from Wednesday to Saturday plus lunch at weekends, : see here .
